# M&A Carve-out & Divestiture Playbook

## When to use this playbook

This is the firm-internal companion to the acquisition-side M&A
playbook. Use it for engagements where the client is the **seller**
of a corporate carve-out (a business unit, geographic region, or
non-core product line being divested from a larger parent), or for
buy-side diligence on a target that is itself a carve-out.

A carve-out diligence is structurally different from a stand-alone
target diligence. The target doesn't operate as a separate business
yet — it shares IT systems, HR, finance, real estate, and often
customers with the parent. Most carve-out value destruction
post-close traces to underestimating the cost of separation; this
playbook structures the diligence so that's not the surprise.

## Eight required diligence threads for carve-outs

In addition to the standard six (financial, commercial, operational,
synergy, valuation, integration), a carve-out diligence MUST cover:

1. **Stand-alone P&L reconstruction** — strip the allocated overhead
   and rebuild the unit's economics as it would operate independently.
   The two most common errors are (a) under-allocating shared services
   it currently consumes for free, and (b) assuming the parent's
   procurement contracts transfer.
2. **Transitional Service Agreement (TSA) scoping** — what services
   the parent must provide the carve-out post-close, for how long,
   at what cost. TSAs are almost always more expensive and last
   longer than the deal model assumes. The base case should plan for
   18-24 months on most services; some (ERP, financial close) can
   stretch to 36.
3. **Customer-contract assignment** — many B2B contracts can't be
   transferred without customer consent. Identify "top 10" customers
   by ARR exposure and map which contracts have explicit
   assignment-clauses vs require renegotiation.
4. **Talent retention scoping** — the carve-out depends on key
   people the parent may not have flagged. Retention packages and
   compete-with-parent restrictions need to be modelled.
5. **IT & data separation** — biggest single source of post-close
   surprise. Estimate the cost of standing up independent
   infrastructure + the timeline for data migration + the risk of
   data-quality loss in the move.
6. **Real estate and shared-site exposure** — does the carve-out
   physically share space with parent operations? What's the exit
   cost from those leases?
7. **Customer perception risk** — how will the customers react when
   the parent's brand backstop is removed? Often the strongest
   defensive moat in B2B is "the parent will still be standing in 5
   years"; the carve-out doesn't have that.
8. **Day-1 readiness** — what minimum must work on Day 1 to keep
   the lights on (billing, payroll, customer support, basic
   security, financial close)? Most other items can extend.

## Valuation considerations specific to carve-outs

Carve-outs typically transact at a 10-25% discount to comparable
stand-alone assets in the same sector. The discount widens when:

- TSA dependence is heavy (>12 months on >5 service categories)
- Customer concentration is high AND contracts lack assignment clauses
- The carve-out's leadership team will not transfer
- The parent retains the technology / IP and is licensing to the
  carve-out (vs transferring outright)
- Shared real estate creates a >12 month exit path

The discount narrows or flips to a premium when:

- The carve-out has its own dedicated leadership already in place
- A clean break is possible operationally (low TSA dependency)
- The carve-out grows faster than the parent (often the case in
  divested innovation units that the parent has under-invested in)
- A strategic acquirer is buying the carve-out for capability +
  customer access, paying the premium for those rather than the unit's
  current economics

## Synergy expectations

Carve-out buyers should be cautious about synergy claims. Two patterns:

- **Cost synergies are typically achievable but slower** than for
  full-company acquisitions because integration starts from a smaller
  base. Plan for 50-65% realisation in year 2, 80-90% in year 3.
- **Revenue synergies are higher-risk** because the carve-out's
  customer base may have weak loyalty to a newly-independent entity.
  Discount revenue synergies by 30-50% versus a comparable stand-alone
  acquisition.

## Walk-away triggers for carve-out buyers

The diligence must surface — and the deal-team agree on — explicit
walk-away triggers BEFORE the IM is shared with seller advisors.
Common triggers we've seen work:

- TSA scope expands by >25% during diligence (signals the parent has
  been undisclosing the dependency)
- Key-person retention slips below 70% of the named-leadership cohort
- A top-3 customer contract is found to require fresh assignment
  consent that the customer has not yet given
- Stand-alone P&L reveals a structurally negative segment that
  allocated overhead was hiding
- IT separation timeline extends past 24 months on the critical path

If any of these triggers fire, the diligence team should write a
formal walk-away memo to the deal team — not a "concern" note — and
the recommendation should swing to REJECT or RENEGOTIATE.

## Process timeline benchmark

A well-run carve-out diligence typically runs:

- Week 1-2: VDR access + initial document review + management
  presentations.
- Week 3-4: Functional diligence streams launch in parallel
  (financial, commercial, ops, IT, HR, legal). Carve-out-specific
  TSA + stand-alone P&L work begins.
- Week 5-7: Customer reference calls + senior-management interviews.
  TSA term sheet drafted.
- Week 8-10: Stand-alone P&L + IT separation cost estimate finalised.
  Synergy quantification with realistic discounting.
- Week 11-13: Integration plan + Day-1 readiness checklist + final
  recommendation.

For comparison, a stand-alone target diligence typically runs 8-10
weeks total; carve-outs add 3-4 weeks because of the separation
diligence threads.
